text: Implement regex matching for a string s and a pattern p. A dot matches any single character, and a star matches zero or more of the preceding element. The match must cover the entire string, not a substring.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the star binds to the character right before it, so a-star is zero or more a's — this is not the shell wildcard where a star matches anything. And it must be a full match?
Exactly — the star is tied to the preceding element, and it's a full match. You can assume every star has a valid preceding character.

Let me run through examples. A-A against a-star is true — two a's. A-B against dot-star is true, since dot-star is any string. And a tricky one — a-a-b against c-star, a-star, b is true: c-star matches zero c's, a-star matches two a's, and b matches b. The zero-match case is the subtle part.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. This problem reminds me of two-string DP — the same grid shape as classic sequence alignment, with one string on each axis. Let dp of i, j mean: does the first i characters of s fully match the first j characters of p. The transition depends entirely on what kind of character p of j minus one is.

Case A — a letter or a dot. If it matches s of i minus one, consume one character from each side and take the diagonal, dp of i minus one, j minus one. Case B — it's a star. It pairs with the character before it as a group, x-star, and two independent ways can succeed, OR'd together. Zero times: dp of i, j minus two — drop the whole group. One or more: x matches s of i minus one, and dp of i minus one, j — eat one s character and keep the group. Here's the part that trips people up — the arrows go different directions. Zero jumps left by two, without touching s. One-or-more jumps up by one, keeping x-star in place so it can eat again. That keep j fixed, move i up is exactly how a star matches many.
Why does one or more need the character check, but zero doesn't?

Because one or more is actually using x to match an s character — so x must be able to match it, equal, or x is a dot. Skip that guard and a-star would gobble any character, effectively becoming dot-star — b against a-star should be false, but you'd wrongly get true. Zero times throws the pattern away without touching s at all, so there's no character to validate. Eat a char, check the char; drop the pattern, don't.

Here's the plan. One: dp of zero, zero is true — empty matches empty. Then seed the first row. An empty s can only be matched by patterns that are all x-star groups taken zero times, so dp of zero, j is true when p of j minus one is a star and dp of zero, j minus two is true, starting at j equals two. The main loop starts at i equals one, so it can't produce this row itself. Two: fill every i and j with case A or case B. Three: return dp of m, n. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. An m plus one by n plus one table, dp of zero, zero true, the first-row loop, then the double loop with the two cases. One thing worth flagging — the one-or-more term reads dp of i minus one, j: the same column, one row up, not the diagonal. That's what lets x-star stay in place and eat again. That's O of m n time and space, and m and n are at most twenty, so it's tiny. A plain recursion without memo is also correct, but blows up exponentially on the star branches — the DP is what tames it.

Let's dry-run a-a-b against c-star, a-star, b — expected true. The column that matters is the a-star column. dp of one, four leans on dp of zero, four for the first a, then dp of two, four leans on dp of one, four for the second a — i climbs, j stays put. Then dp of three, five is true via the b diagonal. That matches. Also checked: b against a-star is false, the character guard; a-b against dot-star is true; and the empty-s cases come from the first row.

Time and space are both O of m n; space compresses to O of n, since each row only needs itself and the row above. Oh, one more thing — the reason this is Hard while a plain two-string DP is Medium is the variable-length match. A letter consumes exactly one input character, one diagonal arrow, but a star can consume zero, left by two, or many, up by one — that variability is what forces multiple transition directions. The shell-wildcard version is actually a touch easier, because its star matches anything and needs no character guard. And I could write this top-down with memoization instead, which reads more directly off the star-means-try-zero-or-try-one definition — same O of m n, lower mental overhead.

Excellent. Three things stood out. You split cleanly on what the pattern character is, and nailed the two star directions. You explained precisely why one or more guards the character and zero doesn't. And you didn't forget the first-row seeding, which is the bug most people ship. That's a strong answer to one of the harder DP problems — strong hire.
